utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis, we've decided that it is in the interests of justice to allow the first part of the statement to be admitted. That would be Exhibit P2480?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraphs 1 to 45. But we're not satisfied it's in the interests of justice to present the rest of the evidence this way, and we are entirely satisfied - which is more important- that we need to hear this evidence because of its potential importance. Now, that may not be much consolation to you, but that is the way in which the evidence of Tanic will have to be conducted. If, of course, something happened along the way that changed the complexion of the written material, then you could try again. But I don't think that's likely, because it's so bitsy, as it were. You have so many different episodes where the link between his knowledge and the original source is not entirely clear. And I have little doubt it's in the general interests of the presentation of a sound case that these links are clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I'll proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This isn't a criticism of the Defence. If we were absolutely sure that cross-examination would pick it all out inadequately, then we would leave it that way. But of course it's not necessarily in the interests of the cross-examiner to clarify everything for your purposes, so we would then have to spend a lot of time clarifying it. So overall we've decided that the best way is to proceed live --.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- from paragraph 46 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: From the contents of 46 onwards. We will, needless to say, be ignoring the statement from paragraphs 1 to 45, and we would welcome a statement that eliminate these paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zyrapi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will continue with your evidence and the cross-examination by Mr. Lukic. Please remember, again, that the solemn declaration continues to apply. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zyrapi.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you rested?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. In law, there is this one rule whereby nobody can promise anything on behalf of another person without that another person consenting to that. There is the exception whereby the Presiding Judge may promise, on behalf of the Defence counsel, something and then that is binding upon that particular counsel. Therefore, we will try to finish this as soon as possible. I would like to go back to the K brigades -- KLA brigades, sorry, along the areas of responsibility. In Drenica, there was the 112th, 113th, and 114th Brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 111, 112, 113, and 114 in Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to make any mistakes anymore. In the Operation Zone Pastrik, which brigades were present?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Operation Zone of Pashtrik, it was 121, 122, 123, 124, and 125.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Dukagjin Operation Zone, which brigades were there?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Dukagjin Operational Zone, there was Brigade 131, 132, 133, 134, and I don't remember other brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was the 35th, 36th, 37th, and 38th as well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 136th, 137th, 138th, I think they came later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Operation Zone of Shala, which brigades were there, please? ?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Operational Zone of Shale, there was brigade 141 and 142.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Lapi Operation Zone?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Operational Zone of Llap, there were brigades 151, 152, and 153.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Operation Zone of Nerodimlje?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Operational Zone of Nerodime, there was 161 and 162.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the Karadak Operation Zone, please?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There, there was Brigade 171.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only the brigades from the operation zone of Drenica and Pastrik were in encirclement that you drew on the map. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones I drew on the map, in the operational zone of Pashtrik, were the brigades operating in that zone. In Drenice, there was the brigade of the operational zone of Drenice and the brigades of the Shale Operational Zone; 141 and 142 I think, in the G zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The other brigades, the remaining four operational zones were mobilised and militarily active at the same time within their combat areas. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the operation zone staff, there was the security service consisting of police units, both military and civilian police, and special units. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the contexts of the zones, there were military police, that's a fact; whereas the special units, rapid intervention units -- yes, but not civilian police, at least not when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Within police, was there the traffic police, prison police, and security police?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember to have separate sections in the police. I know that there was military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that within the KLA military police, there was the so-called Black Hand wearing black uniforms and participating in the actions in the area of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, not when I was serving.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Did the KLA have prisons?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I was in the staff, I don't know. When I was there, there was a prison which was used for disciplinary measures given to various KLA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you are not aware that the KLA had at least 30 prisons in at least 30 municipalities on Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: At least 13 municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no information about what you are putting to me; namely, about prisons in the territories where the KLA was operating. I told you, I don't know about the time before my term of office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'm simply asking you to tell us what you know. We also have information to the effect, or rather, we have the document that the Operations Zone Pastrik, 125th Brigade, number 25-40, where Fejzula Abdulah Ahmeti is being invited to report to Korisa on the 12th of March, 1999, in order to be mobilised into the branches of the KLA. This is the document that says that failure to respond to the summons would incur penalties based on the decree and military law. Do you recall whether the KLA also carried out mobilisations of people and, therefore, did not merely rely on volunteers?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the period I was in office, I don't remember any mobilisation, per se. I know that at a later phase, yes. People were mobilised both within and outside Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 13th of March, 1999, at the markets in Kosovska Mitrovica in Podujevo, explosives were activated by the KLA, resulting in the deaths of civilians only; both Serbs, Albanians, and the Roma. In Kosovska Mitrovica, three women were killed and 39 people injured. At Podujevo, three people were killed, 26 injured. Were these actions ordered by the KLA General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, there was no order by the KLA staff to use explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the action wasn't even approved at a later date by the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn of this action?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned of it, yes. But I don't remember the details of that incident because a long time has passed ever since.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Shaban Shala was one of the commanders of the KLA. At the same time, he was vice-president of the Committee for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms in Kosovo. Do you know in what way the KLA and the Committee For the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms in Kosovo cooperated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is there a basis for the premise for the question, which is that Shaban Shala was both a commander of the KLA and the vice-president?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is a document disclosed to the Defence by the OTP, Operational Zone Drenica. It's ERN number 00100164 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think, nevertheless, there Lukic, you should first of all establish the extent of the witness's knowledge of the positions held by Shaban Shala.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm caught between a hard place and a hammer trying to speed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but when there's an objection to it, you can appreciate we have to do it more carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Mr. Zyrapi, did you know that Mr. Shaban Shala was one of the KLA commanders?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shaban Shala was in the Pashtrik Operational Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the same time he was vice-president of the Committee for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he worked with such issues in the past. But during the period you are putting to me, I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two -- well, are you continuing with the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Committee for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms in Kosovo and KLA cooperated; and if so, in what way?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information on their cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, what position in the Pastrik Operational Zone did Shaban Shala hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Shaban Shala was not in the Pashtrik zone, but in Drenice operational zone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on. A moment ago you said specifically he was in the Pastrik Operational Zone. You want to change that, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I want to change that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He held the position -- he was responsible for civilian and military relations; then after the changes that occurred in March, he held the task of deputy commander of Drenica zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've told us that in the opinion of many Albanians, the war started with the incident at the Jashari homestead. One can look at matters from different angles and see them differently. In our investigations and discussions, conversations, with the other side, we came to the conclusion that the Serbs believed the war to have started with the attack on Orahovac and the surrounding villages. I will not be mentioning names at this time. I know, and I believe, that you do not have any direct knowledge. Nevertheless, I would like to ask you the following: When you came to Kosovo, and especially when you came to be the head of the KLA staff, did you hear from other people that an attack had been carried out on Orahovac and that, in the process, around 80 civilians were abducted and subsequently killed?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April, you asked me when I was Chief of Staff, I heard through the media and then during the period of the trial. But when I asked, when I inquired about that, I didn't receive any accurate information, especially with the Serbs of Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This incident took place in the summer of 1998. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fighting in Rahovec took place during summer of 1998; July, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions on this topic. I would like to elicit a geographical explanation from you. There's something that remained unclear. Is the village of Klecka upon the Berisa mount?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Klecke village is found in the Berisha mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I believe this is my last question. The KLA had members not only in villages but also in towns. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the earlier period. I'm talking about the time I was Chief of Staff. I don't think there were KLA units in the towns. I don't know about 1998, maybe there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you became the Chief of Staff and earlier, did you hear that certain towns and parts of towns such as Orahovac and Suva Reka were even held by the KLA and - let me ask you right away - that there were parts of KLA units in Djakovica definitely?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, during the time I was Chief of Staff, inside Rahovec there were no KLA units, but there were in the periphery, in Suhareke, too. There were KLA units in the villages of Suhareke municipality; in Gjakova municipality, yes, in the villages around Gjakova, but not inside the town. There were no KLA units that operated as such, at least not during the time that I was Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, thank you. And I apologise for the fact that you had to come to the hearing today because of my cross-examination. I have no further questions for you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it that no things we are aware of yet have arisen from the document we disclosed yesterday? I thought I should maybe clarify that, before I begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, do you know the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Unfortunately, no, I don't, because Mr. Ackerman has been dealing with that, and for time being I don't think we have any further questions to raise. I simply didn't have sufficient time to have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I read the document, and indirectly I covered what I had to cover from this document. So our Defence does not have any questions arising from this document anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you should proceed on the assumption, Mr. Marcussen, that there is no issue arising that has so far been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, I would like to ask you for clarification on just a few points of the issues that have come up during your testimony. First, just to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think we should maybe call up exhibit 4D38, if we could, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, this is a document - we will get it up on the screen or maybe we have it - it's a document from the 18th of January, 1999, regarding increase of readiness and placing KLA forces on the highest level of alert. There, we have the document. Maybe I'll just give you a second to look at that. Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was there any particular reason why this order was issued at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I already explained this yesterday. There were combat activities going on in Nerodime Operational Zone during this time; and to my recollection, it was the Recak incident that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Another point I'd like to clarify is something in relation to your function as Chief of Staff. While you were Chief of Staff, who was the head of G3 or operations directorate?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've stated it in my statement, this directorate, the operational directorate, I had exercised this function earlier until March 1999, but my deputy was the one who was carrying the duties in this directorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So you were Chief of Staff and also the director of operations. Is that a correct description?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For a certain period of time until it was determined because there was a lack of officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe the -- the difference between your functions as Chief of Staff and your functions during the relevant period as director of operations, just very briefly maybe so we understand what the two functions are.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two different functions: The operational directorate, in fact, was run by the deputy, and I was running the Chief of Staff. The operational directorate dealt with the operational part, starting with training, development of the KLA structure and operations. So during this period, I mainly focused on the duty of the Chief of Staff, while my deputy was carrying out the duty of the operational directorate. Until the issue of officers was solved, new officers were found appropriate to carry out this function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That answers one-half of that question, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I think thinking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It might be helpful just to have a general statement of the role of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe -- well, the Judge's question: What is -- what was the function of the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The function of the Chief of Staff was to manage and lead the General Staff and the directorates within the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we were going to be a little bit more concrete, what would those tasks consist in, direct and manage?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as Chief of Staff, concrete duties would include preparations to raise the level of training of the staff and the KLA in general operations, disciplinary measures, as well as logistic and procurement issues, high-level of readiness of the staff and the entire KLA personnel. This was, in short, the duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would it be fair also to describe you as head of the administration of the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It includes, partly, the administration of the General Staff as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think things have been fairly cleared, but there's just one thing I would like to touch here on the end, and that is the issue that came up yesterday as to the local staffs. Let me summarise the evidence as I understand it. There were local staffs prior to you becoming Chief of Staff, then the local staffs were incorporated into the structure you put in place with brigade, companies, platoons, and so on. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The staffs existed earlier before I assumed this position, then these staffs were re-organised and incorporated in the frames of companies, brigades, platoons, and other structures in the period 1998/1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you talked about training activities. Did all platoons, did they manage to receive training during the period up to the beginning of the NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that the majority of them were prepared and trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so after -- after the local staffs had been turned into -- had been incorporated into a more military-like structure, would the people who had earlier been in the local staff, would they remain in their villages or would they lodge in other places?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the tasks of the units, platoons, brigades, or companies, part of them would remain, as I said, depending on their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If a platoon was stationed in a village, to your knowledge, would such a platoon have put up some sort of defence line for the village or would that not be the case?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every unit had its defence line and defence positions depending on the configuration of the terrain that would be in the outskirts of the village or outside the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then you also explained that during this period of organising the KLA, you also got more equipment and uniforms and things like that. Were there -- how big a percentage of the ordinary soldiers do you think had uniforms in, say, March 1999?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March 1999, I would say that 85 to 90 percent had military uniforms. The remaining part had sort of improvised uniform, which was not a standard uniform, but which could have been used as uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Those who didn't have -- those who used the improvised uniforms, did they wear the KLA emblem on their improvised uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They all had KLA emblem, regardless of whether it was a standard uniform or improvised one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That concludes my questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marcussen. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That completes your evidence, Mr. Zyrapi. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence and for assisting us. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our next witness is Ratomir Tanic. We have protective measures of image distortion and voice distortion, so I understand we need to take a break for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How long do we need for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I've been told 20 minutes in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's recalculate. Well, what I think we'll do, Mr. Hannis, is we'll break for 20 minutes. We'll resume at ten past 10.00, that's 10.10, and sit until 11.40. And we'll have a half-hour break and resume at 12.10 and sit until 13.40, and I think that would reduce the loss of time as far as possible in the circumstances. So we'll adjourn now until 10.10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, could you stand, please, and could you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the words before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. We'll begin your evidence in the hands of the Prosecution. You'll be examined by Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I should indicate that this witness is testifying as a live witness, but also a portion of his statement will be coming in under Rule 92 ter. And he gives evidence pertinent to paragraphs 17 to 69, 77, and 79 to 101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Exhibit P2480 will be admitted up to paragraph 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, it's my understanding that that version that we've discussed, with the paragraphs that we have deemed can come in under that rule, have now been put in e-court, a version. I would like to hand the defendant -- the witness a copy, the hard copy of the B/C/S version of his statement, so I can ask him the questions under 92 ter requiring him to attest to the fact that he will give the same testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. And this is the one that's now been entered into the system?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have had a copy of that in B/C/S -- my assistant tells me that I do have a copy of that in B/C/S. If I could ask the usher to switch copies with the witness. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And does this have a different number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we propose to submit it under the previous number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can I ask that all other documents be removed from the witness's table, other than the statement that Mr. Hannis gave him, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that there were other documents there. What other documents are there, Mr. Hannis, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know. That may be something the witness brought with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, in court -- just give me a second. Mr. Tanic, in court we will deal only with documents which are presented to you in the course of the examination. If there's a need for you to refer to any other document, then that matter will be raised and dealt with as it arises. So could you please remove from the table in front of you anything other than the document you were handed by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my statement in Serbo-Croat, but that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, I think we can get started.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, what you have in front of you on the table now is a copy of the B/C/S version of your statement containing paragraphs 1 to 47 I believe, the first 11 pages or so of the statement you've seen in a fuller version. Could you have a quick look at that and tell us if you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the record, I think I misspoke. I believe it's paragraphs 1 to 45. Before you came to court today, earlier this week, did you have a chance to review your statement?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And having had that opportunity and noting a couple of minor changes, were you satisfied that the information in there was true and accurate, and you would attest to the Court that you would give the same answers to those questions if you were asked them today?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, can I clarify with you whether you need to switch your microphone off every time you complete a question, or have we a different system?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It was my understanding that when we have voice distortion I need to do that. I don't know if that's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was just that it hadn't been done, but I wondered if we can establish a routine for establishing that it happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I understand is required, and I will be doing that as often as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One of the two changes I think you mentioned in regard to the first 11 pages, one had to do with the names of the persons present during those interviews that took place I think beginning in June of 1999 and ended in July of 2000. You indicated that there was one additional person that was present at one or two of the first sessions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the interviews were held or the conversations were held from June 1999. Yes, another individual was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And without naming that individual, can you tell us what agency or organisation he or she represented.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, that individual represented the British Secret Service, but the individual was there only for the sake of confirming the identity of people from The Hague Tribunal, on the one side, and my identity, on the other side, because we had not previously met. We didn't know each other. And that was the only reason for which that individual was present, since this individual did not participate in any other conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help me with an example of a paragraph where this sort of issue arises?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's only on the first page. There's no paragraph number. It's just at the bottom of the first page. There's a list of persons, all persons attending at the interview. It names Tim Kelly, Dennis Milner, and Alexandra Milenov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The other one you pointed out, Mr. Tanic, relates to I believe paragraph 10; and in your statement it says: "I reported," and you had weekly meetings with the SDB. I think you wanted to indicate the name of your primary contact. Can you tell us who that person was at SDB?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: I could only say that in private session. As far as I know this person is still in active service, and the identity of the person isn't known. But I was thinking of the deputy chief of the security service Mijatovic and Jovica Stanisic, well, these individuals are well-known individuals. I suggest that this person be named in private session in order to protect the security, the safety, of that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tanic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May we do that, Your Honour, for the purpose of naming this primary contact at SDB?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, that seems appropriate. Let's go into private session for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, could I -- with those changes, are you willing to attest to the Court that your statement in those 10 or 11 pages, paragraphs 1 to 45, is true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge and information?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, could you give us a little of your background information. Could you tell us where you were born?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1956 in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: I'm a Yugoslav. I was born in Yugoslavia, but naturally I'm a Serb, thanks to the unfortunate events that transpired in my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you attend high school in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I can summarise my educational background since I completed part of my education in my own country, part abroad. In my own country I completed secondary economics school, secondary school for economy. I studied sociology, economy, and philosophy, and I passed a significant number of exams. Abroad, I completed the gymnasium and I also graduated, or rather, I obtained an MA in political science. I have an BA and an MA in political science, and I also graduated from a college for police science. So my educational background is quite broad and has a dual nature, since I completed a significant part of my education abroad, in the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with regard to your degrees in political science, did you obtain those since the end of the war and being relocated?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I started my MA in political science, and I obtained my diploma for police science under a different name, once I had been relocated and once I was able to focus a little on my education.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you were in Serbia, did you perform your national service, as required?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, when I was 27. I was born in 1956, so I was 26 or 27 years old. It was at the beginning of the 1980s. It was in 1980 or 1981, something like that. I was 25 or 26 when I went to serve in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And between approximately the mid-1970s and the early 1990s, apart from your year of mandatory service, what kind of work did you engage in, or what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: I worked as a tradesman in some sort of federal institution. I was involved in commercial affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During this period, did you also begin doing some work or having some operational relationship with the SDB?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time I already had a relationship with the Serbian SDB. Since the age of 22 or 23, I did have a relationship with them, a working relationship, exclusively. I slowly started performing such duties at a fairly insignificant level, at least initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you explain the acronym for me. Sometimes we have used the term "SDB" and sometimes the term "RDB." Can you give us the expansion for both of those and explain the difference, if any, between those two?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, none of the acronyms are quite correct, since the official name of the service is the Sector of the State Security Service, so the correct acronym would be the RSDB; however, the SDB acronym was widely used, although the official name of the body was as I've just relayed to you. This -- because the service was part of the MUP, of the police, system, and that's why it was called the Sector for State Security or the Sector of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was the SDB that you were associated with, was that a body that was under the Republic of Serbia or the FRY or which?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Under the Republic of Serbia. We had, or rather, I had very rare work contacts with the Federal State Security Service, so the service at hand is the Serbian service. And let me tell you at once that this was no espionage; it was just a normal process of recruitment and training of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask, how long did your working relationship with the SDB last, from when to when?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify working relationship, as a term. I was not employed with the State Security Service. I was their external associate, and afterwards I was upgraded within cooperation. Our work contacts, however, lasted ever since I turned 22 or 23, although intermittently, whenever there was nothing to do, there would be an interruption in our cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would it be wrong to have formed the impression that you would be a source of intelligence for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It wouldn't be wrong. The only difference being that the -- this was a two-way information flow. I also received a sort of practical training from them, and very often we assessed information and -- rather than just exchange information. But your impression would be quite true, that they also received information from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it from your current circumstances that your relationship with them ended at some point in time. Can you tell us when that occurred.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the break in late 1980s or the one in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please tell me about both.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: In late 1980s and in early 1990s, as you know, the multi-party system was introduced to Yugoslavia, and I wanted to make sure that my cooperation with the State Security Service would not be used against my friends in my political life. There was a pause there, after which I received guarantees that my contacts, which had to do with the international sphere and Kosovo, would never be used against my friends and that I would never be sought to give them information to that effect, even after the introduction of the multi-party system. After I received this piece of information we continued cooperation. The break in 1999 took place after my wife and I were kidnapped off the street. We were tortured; and in my assessment, this was the preparation for my murder. Fortunately, this happened at the same time when -- fortunately for me, this happened at the same time when there was the attempted assassination on Draskovic; and after that, we used the situation to leave the country. We had a terrible misunderstanding on the Kosovo issue and this was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. We'll come back and ask you some more about that later on. Some time then after that initial break in your contacts, did you become politically active after the multi-party system was established?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I taught the subject of the multi-party system; and because I became politically active, I asked that I receive guarantee -- guarantees that my work, my intelligence work, would not be used against me in my political work. But however, they were not really interested in that bit at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So what was your first involvement in? Did you join a particular political party or group?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: At the very outset, I became one of the junior co-founders - if I can put it that way - or perhaps I could just say that I joined them. This was the Association for the Yugoslav Democratic Initiative, and then I became a junior co-founder of one of the political parties. However, my first engagement was in the Association for the Yugoslav Democratic Initiative. This was a non-nationalist opposition party, the first of the sort in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when was that? How long did you stay with them?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: This took place toward the very end of, or rather, no, to -- at the very start of the 1990s, in early 1990s. I can't really recall the year, and I don't think it's -- well, perhaps in 1991, but not later than 1991. I spent some two years working also on international relations; and then together with a group of prominent opposition members, I took part in the establishment of the Civic Alliance of Serbia. And I can safely say that I am one of the junior co-founders of that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Briefly, what was the Civic Alliance?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Another non-nationalist opposition party, highly respectable, gathering people, many of whom in 2000, later on in 2000 took part in the toppling of the government in Serbia. Some of them were my political students, and not only mine of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long did you stay with the Civic Alliance?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: I was vice-president of the Civic Alliance of Serbia, one of the two or three vice-presidents in charge of international relations, and I held that position until 1994/1995, when I accepted the position of the special advisor to the president of New Democracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have described the two parties that you were associated with as non-nationalist opposition parties. Did you never envisage being in power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was done with New Democracy. When I went over to New Democracy, they became part of the ruling coalition with Milosevic's party and JUL. Therefore, from 1994/1995, I was no longer part of the opposition, rather, I was special advisor to the president of one of the three ruling parties in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was your boss, sir, who was the head of the New Democracy?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Dusan Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the position of the ND, the New Democracy, in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Just as JUL, the Yugoslav United Left, we were the junior partners in the tripartite coalition. Milosevic's party, the SBS, was the main force in the coalition; whereas we formed -- we were actually junior partners in the coalition, that's to say New Democracy and JUL. We had our deputy prime ministers, our own men in international relations and Kosovo affairs, but of course the balance of power or the division of powers wasn't really on equal terms because a large share was in the hands of Milosevic's party. However, it was a veritable coalition because we had won seats at the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to the coalition, who was the head of the JUL party, the Yugoslav Left party?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Milosevic's wife, Mira Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall now the relative size of the three parties in the coalition, in terms of numbers of seats in the parliament?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, you know how it is. Matters are not that simple in Serbia. If we look at the number of seats in the parliament, it was pretty low, the number of seats we had. We had I think only six or seven deputy seats. They were, of course, important in order to have the majority. But absolutely speaking, we had a small number of seats, although one always has to look at the power that the individual parties enjoyed on the ground, because the power in Serbia is always different from -- has to be distinguished from institutional powers, at least this is how the matters stood in Milosevic's Era.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the relative size of JUL versus the SPS?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: JUL was -- I think you ought to switch off your --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: JUL was the junior partner, as we were. In home affairs and in business, they had disproportionately high powers, given their political weight. Because in political weight, you first have the SPS, then New Democracy carried more political weight than JUL. But in economic affairs, as I said, JUL dominated in Serbia, though our weight was quite prominent in terms of the Kosovo affairs -- well, in terms of us being able to exert certain influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In terms of that division of power within the coalition, what did New Democracy get? Was there a particular area that you had responsibility for?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Except for the seats in the republican and federal parliaments, New Democracy and JUL were working hard toward the turning point in the peace process, because Milosevic and some of his associates, like Milutinovic, promised -- but primarily Milosevic, that there would not be a war, that he didn't want to cause any more wars, that he realised that one could achieve with peaceful means much more for Serbia. And he wanted to make this turning point toward peace and that he needed political advisors who would slowly prepare the transition of Serbia's policies from war toward peace. In Serbia, the greatest problem was Kosovo. This is something that Milosevic's associates repeated later on. He specifically engaged New Democracy and, partly, JUL to prepare the political settlement for the Kosovo issue and engaged us in some international areas, such as our rapprochement with the Council of Europe, our relations, and establishing of understanding with western partners. I myself was engaged on a number of activities, together with the president of my party, of course. Therefore, these were our duties strictly authorised by Milosevic. Of course, they overlapped with our convictions because New Democracy also advocated the peaceful policies, as did the Civic Alliance of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You previously testified in the Milosevic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall that Mr. Milosevic challenged whether or not you were a member of New Democracy or only a sympathiser. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this was just a fantasy.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I object to the leading form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I object to the leading form of the question, and I -- this is very close to challenging this witness's evidence as opposed to leading it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We disagree with that, Mr. O'Sullivan. We do not consider this to be an inappropriate question and we'll allow it. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness next Exhibit P695.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, at the time that you left the Civic Alliance and went to New Democracy, was there a -- was there an article about that in a local paper?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: This event was widely reported on in the domestic press. There wasn't just one article, there were at least 30 or 40 articles on that because I had by that time become a prominent member of Civic Alliance and a person advocating the Dayton peace. They thought it a big deal that I had moved from Civic Alliance to New Democracy. In fact, it wasn't a big deal. It was just a technical issue, but still, there were 30 to 40 articles reporting on that. At the same time, this was the only transfer from one political party to another, which wasn't accompanied by mudslinging or offences, because I did not speak negatively about my previous party, nor were there any particular affairs related to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, do you see that article on the screen in front of you, or do we have to scroll down? I can't read the Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a bit further down. Yes. [In English] Yeah, it's okay. [Interpretation] Yes. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we put the English version on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there some significance in this point, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour. I hope it will become apparent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, which newspaper was this reported?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is Politika, the official newspaper that was under -- fully controlled under Milosevic's or by Milosevic's regime. It wasn't independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as reported herein, did you join the Executive Council of New Democracy?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Right from the start, I was a member of the core leadership. I was a member of the Executive Council and a special advisor. It's a bit immodest of me to say that, but I have to say that I was a big political star who transferred from one political party to another. And this was done on clear grounds. The advocating of the Dayton peace and the pursuing of a peaceful policy by Serbia on the basis of the Dayton peace. I did not make this transfer because of money or anything of the sort, but because the survival of Serbia was at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try and ask you to do your best to confine your answers to my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it would be very difficult to regard this as authentic in any way. It doesn't look like a newspaper report. It's not in the language in which it was published. I don't know if you're relying on it. The witness's answers deal with the matter. The document itself seems to me, at least, to be neither here nor there, unless you claim it's something different from what the witness was suggesting it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, did you see the Cyrillic version of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That normally comes on the screen, but I haven't got that, no. That's my -- sorry. That should have been on the screen, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was up initially, Your Honour, and then I asked for the English so I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My apologies. The position is now clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tanic, if I may, I just want to go through the portions of your statement Exhibit 2480, which are in just to ask for clarification on a couple of matters. In paragraph 2 of your statement, you make mention to the fact that in late 1999, you were preparing a book on Yugoslav politics related to the Kosovo crisis. Did you ever complete that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: About the Serbian role in the Kosovo issue and the provoking of the war there. I didn't complete anything, because the collecting of the documentation for the book and my intention to write the book was the immediate cause of my subsequent kidnapping. I didn't manage to finish it, and now I'm not in the position to do that because I'm under the witness protection programme and I'm not entitled to publish anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, you talk about how you got authorisation to participate in what you refer to as discreet negotiations regarding Kosovo. And you say you received this authorisation from Milosevic in a meeting that you and Dusan Mihajlovic had with him. Can you tell us where that meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: In Mr. Milosevic's office. Mihajlovic and I introduced Milosevic to our plan for the settlement of the Kosovo issue. The plan was one of the basis for -- was the basis for all the subsequent peacemaking plans, and, as always happened at such meetings, Milosevic approved that. This was a three-phased plan which appeared elsewhere on several occasions on some other bases. The main point was to try and solve the Kosovo issue by political means before a war breaks out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, you mentioned that this proposal for you to participate in these negotiations was accepted by the SDB from a security perspective. When and how was that done, that they accepted it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: This happened right away in 1995. The SDB was headed by Jovica Stanisic at the time, and they were very much interested in finding a political settlement that would avert a war in Kosovo. And they were quite content with having me in the company of people who would be conducting these negotiations. There wasn't just me, just to make this clear, there were five or six other people involved in the negotiations as well. They authorised it through the service leadership in 1995; of course in security terms, because they were interested in the security aspect of the political negotiations. Most, or rather, in preventing armed conflicts in Kosovo. So of course they wanted to have a political settlement that would avert war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, paragraph 5, you mentioned that other Serb participants in the negotiations included Mr. Ratko Markovic, who was the deputy prime minister of the Republic of Serbia, and Mr. Dojcilo Maslovaric, who was the Yugoslav envoy to the Vatican, yet you describe yourself as the principal negotiators. Your position was more junior to theirs, why do you call yourself the principal negotiator in these discreet negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, this is just the terminological difference between Serbian and English. Of course, the principal negotiator was Ratko Markovic; however, he was completely unsuccessful. He didn't take the negotiations seriously and merely carried out the orders given by Milosevic and his associates. Maslovaric, was, for instance, much more successful than him. I called myself the principal negotiator -- well, I wasn't the main negotiator, officially. But together with the president of my party, Dusan Mihajlovic, I was the most successful because we brought about the most important results in trying to find a political settlement in Kosovo which was satisfactory to Serb. Now I'm speaking about myself. I had enough freedom to openly speak with the western factors and Russians. I also had the support of the State Security Service, which other members of the negotiating team lacked. Therefore, judging by our performance, my performance was the best, mine and President Dusan Mihajlovic's. In those terms, you could say that I was the best negotiator. Eventually, such a balance of powers was set up that whenever a problem needed to be issued with Milosevic, Milosevic would either solve it on his own with Milutinovic or he would address Mihajlovic and myself. The other negotiators were not that successful. They served as couriers mostly, although they did achieve something. So formally and legally speaking, up until 1997, it was Ratko Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regarding your efforts in these negotiations in paragraph 11, you indicate that your progress and any difficulties you had were presented to Milosevic in three different ways, one of them being through regular SDB reports. Do you know how often those reports about your progress went to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, in my rough assessment, every two or three months -- or every three or four months such reports would be forwarded to him. Several times a year, in any event, because I worked quite intensively. On the issue, I obtained significant results. The SDB was very satisfied, and I had direct contact via Mijatovic and Stanisic, or rather, Mijatovic would forward the report to Stanisic and Stanisic to Milosevic. And I know for sure that Milosevic would make use of what he received as well as his associates, because I received feedback information through my service and through the leader of my party, Dusan Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you said you received feedback information. What was the feedback you were getting about the progress you were making in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, there was much praise of myself and Mihajlovic. But I'm testifying on my own behalf, that's why I'm only mentioning myself now. But we had advanced three or four five years, in fact. Milosevic himself didn't believe that certain things could be obtained but we were successful nevertheless. So I had carte blanche to examine any possible solution. That's the amount of success we had. Naturally, later on the price we had to pay for this was very high. Mihajlovic also received feedback information. Under different circumstances, we wouldn't have been able to work in this way for three years. If we hadn't been authorised to work in such a way and if things hadn't been functioning properly, we wouldn't managed to do this work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you give me an example of something that you achieved in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, above all, we introduced a third party in the negotiations. This was a very complicated problem because Milosevic did not want the third party in the negotiations to be represented by a state or group of states. As a result, Mihajlovic and I - and again, I'm just speaking about myself right now - I tried to find influential NGOs or other groups that had ties to the government but were nevertheless not governmental bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've read about that in your statement. I was wondering if there was actually any success you could identify in the actual conduct of the negotiations, rather than in the setting up of the parties for negotiating purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as for specific successes, our greatest success for our party was the fact that in the course of the negotiations the Albanian side engaged in a minimum of terrorist activity. That can be seen from the relevant documents. There were only sporadic incidents. And then secondly, the Albanian side, although they never gave up the idea of independence, they in fact agreed to postpone this issue and to create the conditions for some sort of a 15-year transition stage. So finally the agreement itself was our greatest success, this draft agreement, which was similar to the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement, an agreement that they signed. So everything had been prepared for that solution, but it wasn't implemented. These are some examples of political success, but, Your Honours, you should bear in mind the fact we were doing all we could to avoid a war. So we believe that we are successful if we manage to find political ways of avoiding war at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps I've missed this, but are you saying there's a document that was signed by the Albanian side agreeing to a 15-year transition stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, there is no such documents. But there are documents that quite clearly show the intention of the Albanian side to accept temporary political agreement, transition political agreement, and that wouldn't cover just a three-month period, that's for sure. This could be seen from a number of their documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I show the witness a document that pertains to Your Honour's question, I hope. Exhibit P2481.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While that's coming up, Mr. Tanic, I wanted to ask you, you mentioned the importance of introducing a third party into the negotiations between yourselves and the Kosovo Albanians. At the start of your assignment in this area, I think you indicated in your statement there were two things that Milosevic insisted on with regard to these discreet negotiations. Can you tell us what those two terms were?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: The first condition was that the political solution should not directly lead to the secession of Kosovo, rather its independence or its full state independence. And the second condition was that a third party should participate, and that would be an NGO. But according to what Milosevic and his associates said, anything else was possible, and that included substantial autonomy, et cetera, et cetera. Later we saw that all of this was in fact not true, but that's another story.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of a third party, what was the position of the Kosovo Albanians about having a third party in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, they accepted this, reluctantly, but they accepted it. What were they to do? Negotiations are always difficult when such issues are at stake. I don't believe that they were always satisfied with the way we moved ahead, but they had to accept certain things. So they accepted a third party. They would rather have governments involved, but they accepted the participation of influential NGOs in the negotiation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know why they would have preferred to have a government rather than an NGO?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, they wanted firmer guarantees for the political negotiations, and governments can provide better guarantees. On the other hand, as I have already explained -- or as I explained to the western elements that I've discussed matters with, to find a peaceful solution for Kosovo is not a simple matter. You have to prepare negotiations very well if they are to be successful. You can't prepare negotiations with governments. This is never done anywhere in the world. Negotiations -- always negotiations that are held at a less official level. So they accepted this proposal, naturally, but reluctantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know why Mr. Milosevic had a preference for an NGO, as opposed to a third government or a third party in the form of an international government?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, so that he could later say that the negotiations were not serious negotiations, that it was just a discussion between intellectuals, that everything was unofficial. So it was in order to be able to dismiss the negotiations. Negotiations that his closest associates and he himself participated in, in fact, because this process went on for about three or three and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you to take a look at the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you go on. Is it not commonplace in the world for national governments to resist the involvement of third-party governments in their own internal affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is common; however, the Kosovo problem had a strong international dimension. And as far as I know, Milosevic was not really very involved in the issue of sovereignty. He was more involved in the fact that it was difficult for him to deal with this. But naturally, there is the problem of sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I'm interested in the leap that you then make to say that this was a deliberate choice so that the negotiations would not succeed. Now, that's a -- not necessarily a logical leap for me on the information you've presented so far.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I didn't say so that the negotiations wouldn't succeed, but so that Milosevic could subsequently dismiss them or distance himself from them if he wanted to do so. If the negotiations were successful, then all the credit would go to Milosevic and his associates. If the negotiations failed to succeed, well, then he could say that these were just intellectual discussions, discussions amongst intellectuals. This is a fairly common technique that is employed throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you see, that puts a completely different complexion on your evidence, because the way you initially answered the question, it was on the basis that there was only one potential outcome, that the negotiations would be dismissed. Now you're saying that he would only wish to distance himself if they failed, and that clarifies it for me. I now understand the position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, could you now take a look at the document that's on the screen and tell us if you recognise what that is.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, the document is called, "Jointly Agreed Positions." It concerns the Serbian and Albanian side. It's a document from New York. It's one of the many documents that was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is one that you refer to in paragraph 32 of your statement. You say this was a result with your negotiations up to this point in time as sort of the ground rules for the negotiations between the parties?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Fine. Yes. This represented some of the results obtained. Naturally, we obtained more significant results, but this document, nevertheless, shows that the Albanian side was prepared to accept a political solution. However, I have to point something else out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I received this piece of paper but there's no signature, there's nothing on it. It can't be a document. It can't be accepted as a document anywhere in the world. I can type something out at home and then pretend it's a document. Does it have a signature or a title? Can this be treated as a document? If so, fine, I have nothing against that. But I'm just asking this as a matter of principle. What is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The difference here is that the witness himself is identifying this as a document in the compilation of which he participated, and therefore a signature is not an essential requirement for authenticity in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be fine if it was his document, but he's talking about jointly held positions. So this concerns a number of individuals and that is why I raised this objection. If it was Mr. Tanic's position, well everything would be fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I clarify this matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will be asked some more questions in a moment. Mr. Fila, in case there is doubt about authenticity, Mr. Hannis will explore it a little bit further and clarify it, but my impression was that the witness was party to these, the negotiations which led to the compilation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you heard the Judge's comments. Were you a participant in the production of this document?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked on the preparation of the document. I wasn't in New York, though, but the leader of my party, Dusan Mihajlovic, was there and I also participated in preparing other documents. The negotiations were held in secret, and, naturally, the documents that were related to those negotiations were not signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the question really is: What is this document? That's a question for you, Mr. Tanic. What is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, okay. It is a document. It's one of several documents through which the Albanian side demonstrates that it is prepared to find a peaceful political solution to the problems in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did you acquire it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mihajlovic gave it to me when he returned from New York. Representatives of the American Ministry of Foreign Affairs were there. Agani was there, too; he was the number two man in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are adequate indications of the authenticity of this to be an exhibit in this case with the number P2481. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would note, Your Honour, also this document has the identifier on the English version as item TX-7, which is the one that's referred to in paragraph 32 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The handwritten -- the handwritten TR item TX-7 is referred to in paragraph 32 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, if I can understand, this -- these three paragraphs were the result of negotiations that had been going on for some time?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And it also concerns a far broader document. There are at least 20 witnesses who can say that this was agreed on by the Serb and Albanian associates in New York. There are some associates of Madeleine Albright, for example, and Madeleine Albright, herself, and I could identify another person in the afternoon. I would have to check my agenda. There was Mihajlovic, Raskovic on our side; I think there was Vesna Pesic there, as well as many witnesses as you could wish for. And this document is fully authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You say, in paragraph 32, that Mr. Mihajlovic and Fehmi Agani went to New York to somehow formalise this agreement. Do you know, was there a separate document that was signed, or was it because of the nature of these discreet negotiations that there are no signatures? Do you know the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: No. There were no signatures, no documents, because, as I said, the negotiations were discreet. At the time the American side wanted to have something more concrete on paper, so Mihajlovic on the part of the governing coalition and Agani on behalf of the government went to New York to do this. But there's another piece of paper that has been signed, but I don't want to get ahead of myself. So I assume that we'll be dealing with that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I do want to move forward in the negotiations from this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that. You described the second point in this document as representing Kosovo Albanians' agreement to step back from independence. How do you read that into the second point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this can't be seen in this document. I know that they accepted to step back from that or postpone independence for a long period of time. I know that on the basis of conversations, but I do agree that this document doesn't demonstrate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nor did Albanians or -- nor were Albanians able to put that into any of their documents, just as we couldn't put into these documents everything that we wanted. This was a very difficult and sensitive issues, the positions of the two sides were far apart; and as a result of that, some matters were not put on paper because of the public at home, which is quite understandable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you go on to say in your statement that Milosevic accepted this pre-agreement. Are you suggesting that he had accepted the second point in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, absolutely. In the period between 1994 and 1997, Milosevic behaved as if he was fully involved in trying to find a solution of the Kosovo issue together with his associates, but that is valid only for that period of time between 1994 and 1997. It was only occasionally in the course of 1997 that he started to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So -- started to what? Do we not have a complete answer? Could you just tell us again the end of your answer. The interpreters missed something. The transcript says: "It was only occasionally in the course of 1997 that he started to ..." Could you complete that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only in the second half of 1997, he started giving away some telltale signs, as did his associates, that a political solution would not come into effect; whereas in 1998, definitely he and his associates turned toward a war solution and the provoking of a war in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be you didn't entirely understand my question. The second point on this document is a reference to negotiations starting with "no pre-conditions." Now, are you saying that Mr. Milosevic accepted no pre-conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I understood your question. He accepted no pre-conditions, whereas everywhere in the world -- yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that would mean no pre-condition that Kosovo should remain a part of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, nobody believed that Kosovo would remain part of Serbia. First of all, the discussion was that it would become -- that it would remain part of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, that's a helpful comment, but please try to confine yourself to answering the question. The reason it becomes a bit blurred, of course, is because you describe the second point in your statement as representing the Kosovo Albanians' agreement to step back from independence, which would suggest that they were accepting a pre-condition. And therefore, an element of confusion comes into the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In negotiations surrounding such matters, there are always quite a few misunderstanding. Of course one could conclude, from point 2, that they gave up their requests, because previously they always said that they wanted independence or nothing. One -- when we read here that they gave up any pre-conceived or possible outcomes of negotiations, yes, one could conclude that they stepped back from their request for independence; hence, my conclusion in the statement.
