utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, at the beginning of these negotiations, wasn't that the biggest stumbling block to even get started, that is the question about the status of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're gesturing with your hand, but I don't know what that means.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Can you please switch off your microphone. Yes. Of course, the first problem was to even broach discussions, to start negotiations. Another problem was that the positions of the parties were far apart, and one had to at least work toward bringing them closer together. The pre-condition for that, of course, was even to start negotiating.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And they were far apart on the issue of Kosovo's status in what way exactly? What was the position of the Kosovo Albanians about the status of Kosovo? What did they want when you were trying to start these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: I appeal to the Trial Chamber to understand the need to give a more extensive explanation. In negotiations, every side tries to gain as much as they can from the other side. The Albanians only spoke of independence of Kosovo; whereas, we spoke, the Serbian side, spoke of the limited autonomy in Serbia. In the negotiations process, it was quite clear that none of the sides were able to achieve their maximum demands or extreme positions, and I know that the Albanians were aware of that. I can say that because I spoke to them, and I know that the western community was against such extremist positions from Albanians. This meant that both sides had to give up on their quite extreme positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And give up forever or just temporarily so discussions could go forward?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: I will be quite frank. What Mihajlovic and I told Milosevic, and what I told the security service, the State Security Service, and which was the only wise tactics for Serbia, and this was that we should try to outwit the Albanians. Not to win them, but to outwit them. Therefore, we drafted a plan, which we advocated, and that was to achieve a temporary political settlement over the period of some ten to 15 years. In the meantime, we would become a member of the European Union. At that time, in 1997/1998, the Union was strongly in favour of that, unlike today. And we said, Okay. If the Albanians want to secede Serbia and Yugoslavia, then they have to secede from the European Union; and if they want to, they can try. We simply wanted to give the Albanians the economic carrot, which would induce them to give up their political demands. They were aware of that; the realised that and they knew that this was their reality. They would rather become members of the European Union than to create a circus surrounding independence, because the political reality would be quite different. Our negotiations were geared toward politically outwitting the Albanians; that was our approach. For this reason, the Albanians said, Very well. If this is the path toward European Union, then what can we do about it? This is our destiny. At the time the west exerted strong pressure on them to give up on their ultra-nationalist positions. They agreed to that at the time with hesitation, I have to say, reluctantly. Whether this would be a lasting solution or not, I am under the impression that had this been successful this would have been -- would have proved to be a permanent political settlement. At the time, the Albanians didn't have a KLA. They weren't organised. They existed mostly abroad; however, at that point Milosevic decided to give up on the political process and started provoking incidents and conflicts in Kosovo, together with his associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's a good point for a break, Your Honour, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Tanic, we have to have a break at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll need to go into closed session while the witness leaves the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When we broke, sir, we were talking about this sort of a pre-agreement for the negotiations that dealt, in a way, with the stumbling block about the issue of Kosovo status. What -- can you describe the process for us in terms of the negotiations from that point. What was your approach? What did you agree on about how to approach negotiating this issue?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: No. These were already full-blown negotiations. There was the preparation for very short negotiations where Milosevic and Rugova would take part and produce a complete agreement; therefore, these were already negotiations, not preparations for them. Because, of course, we had to have this preliminary part, we couldn't expect Milosevic and Rugova to meet for 30 times before they come up with an agreement. Milosevic got this text where he knew already that the European Union and the United States supported the document, and he was supposed to prepare together with his associates for the signing of the agreement with Rugova. We didn't have to do anything about it, because we already had this three-phase agreement in our hands, which cropped up on several occasions afterwards and, among other occasions, in the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You talk about that three-phase approach in your statement in paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can we show the witness Exhibit 704, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you recall now what those three phases were and describe them in short terms. The first phase was?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: The first phase comprised a number of confidence-building measures in the area of education, health care, sports, and joint security. These were the classic confidence-building measures, also involving education, health care, and sports. The second phase provided for a temporary political settlement of the crisis, which was the must sensitive one, and of course the implementation of the agreement. The third phase was the definite status of Kosovo, but of course this bridge was to be crossed by the time we reached it, after the political agreement is reached. It had to be there in order for both sides to save face and to be able to defend the agreement at home in the sense and in the meaning which it had in political terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, where is this in the statement? Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 16, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, should I address that question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you see that document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: On the screen, I see the text written by Mr. Surroi. But I don't see anything which has to do with what I've been defending in the negotiations as our, so to speak, official approach; namely, the three-phase settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If we can put the English on the screen. I think we've got the wrong B/C/S translation associated with this document. Yes. The English is the one that I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you read and understand English?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I graduated from my studies in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. For purposes of this document, can you look at the English and tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes. This is the document produced under the auspices of one of the NGOs involved in the process. It is the Bertelsmann Foundation. The document was adopted at the talks in Halki and Munich. Kinkel and Vedrine, the German and French foreign ministers supported the document and presented it to the European Union which accepted this as the basis. Monsignor Paglia was also involved at the time as the representative of the Kosovo contact group. He was privy to that and in full agreement with it. It was all -- it was all dealt with at this level. This is to say, that this document is not merely a document of an NGO, but is a document which served as the basis for negotiations involving the international community. This document contains the three-phase solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page of this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, this document on the cover page was dated --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, excuse me. I'm sorry, Your Honours, for interrupting. But there is again a problem with the transcript that I heard clearly that the witness said something about "the low-key," but it's not in the transcript. And he said it in English, and that's why. I believe after the -- it's 54, 5 and 6. It was all dealt with at this level, something "low-key."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, did you use the expression "low-key" somewhere in your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Because, from the very start, I've been saying that the negotiations were semi-secret and that in order for Milosevic to be able to dismiss them in the future if he found them to be unsatisfactory. But in order to avoid any confusion, I wanted to clearly say, also for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, that this was not merely an NGO document, but that this was a document that was subsequently defended before the European Union by Kinkel and Vedrine in order to provide the basis for further associations, and also by Monsignor Paglia. And we always negotiated at this low level. When I say "low level," it was semi-secretive so that if anyone made the wrong move, Milosevic and his associates could -- well, this is normally done worldwide. This is the way things are done abroad. Mr. Milutinovic is a professional diplomat, and he knows what the practice in this regard is and he can confirm that. And I believe he became the foreign minister in 1997, and he was informed about this when the international community said "all right" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you, Mr. Tanic. You must confine your answers to the particular questions we're asking. We have a lot of material. We have the three points here, and we've a long way to go in this evidence. So, please, try to control your answers to the -- so that they are confined to the questions raised. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we could go to page 4 of this document, it's two pages on from where we are. No, I'm sorry. I misspoke, Your Honour. I have an excerpt. It's actually page 69, I believe. In my hard copy, I just printed out the particular excerpt relating to Mr. Tanic's contribution to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It's referred to in his own statement, and we'll read the particular passage in due course, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. One more page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'll just ask you one question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, is that a document that you wrote that was a part of this paper at the Munich conference in August of 1999 -- or 1997, my mistake?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is one of the documents I drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And in there you described the three-phase process that you had -- that you and the others involved in the negotiations had been using to approach this problem?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the same document that Mihajlovic and I showed to Milosevic in 1995 and familiarised him with it. It is the same type of document. It's not word for word the same document, but that's the initial document that we have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to move on to paragraph 19 of your statement, where you talk about the participants in the negotiations. You mentioned that you had numerous meetings with Fehmi Agani in the process. Were those meetings one on one?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Some five or six meetings were indeed one on one, especially so at the time when we were trying to find a formula on the basis of which the Albanians would give up on their autonomy, whilst not undermining their position vis-a-vis the Albanian extremists. These negotiations were led and meetings were held in Pristina; whereas, there were other meetings where some other persons would be present, most often -- well, I've given you my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You also say in that paragraph that at the end of 1997, Mr. Milosevic cancelled these discreet negotiations. Can you tell the Judges how that came about. How did he cancel them?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: He did not cancel only the negotiations. But Milosevic's regime, Milosevic and his associates, rejected the entire process which we supported and worked on between 1994 and 1997. He did that in several ways. First, he held a speech in Pristina, where he said that there was no way in which autonomy would be restored. Then several months later, he retracted his positions; and then in his conversations with foreign ambassadors, he said that this statement on his part was done for some internal purposes and that the negotiations would go on. However, Dusan Mihajlovic and I, since we were known in Serbia as the main protagonists of the Serbian settlement of the Kosovo issue, we were told not to engage in that at all. There would be no discussion, the entire political solution fell through, and there would be a war. Milosevic and some of his associates provided some quite incomprehensible arguments in favour of a war because a peaceful political settlement was in Serbia's interests. We can talk about this later. At any rate, I received personally from Milosevic, and through the security service and through Mihajlovic, I received signals -- or actually orders that we should give up on this political project and that there would be a war. So this was the deterioration of the situation leading to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you give this Court some specifics about when or how you got these orders to stop trying to negotiate a political settlement?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: It's quite difficult to pin-point that. It happened on several occasions, and it was a process rather than an event. I know for a fact that Mihajlovic summoned me one day and told me, Rato - this was the way they addressed me - the entire matter fell through. Milosevic doesn't want to negotiate, he wants a war, I spoke to him, and so on and so forth. At one reception Milosevic told me, all furious, that nothing would come out of these negotiations, that he would prove that there are less than one million Albanians in Kosovo. All of a sudden this issue of the size of the Albanian population became topical. This was an informal conversation. I didn't have a chance to ask him to clarify. Later on in our discussions with Mr. Milutinovic as well, we were able to see that nothing would come out of it; not because of Mr. Milutinovic's wishes, but because of the orders from Mr. Milosevic. Finally, the security service also told me to take care of keeping a head on my shoulders rather than getting involved in these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have a problem with the translation. This entire discussion between the witness and the -- and Milosevic was at a reception organised in a July. I don't think that is in the transcript, and I think it's very important so that we can really place this witness's testimony in the appropriate context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you say the date is missing?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours, not just the date, but also the occasion on which this discussion was held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The occasion -- line 5 on page 58 gives the occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, JUL, J-U-L, is a political party. It's not the month July; it's the Yugoslav United Left. So it was a reception at J-U-L, which means the political party, J-U-L, the political party, and not "Jul," as we say in our language, which is the month of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. J-U-L receptions were always held in July. The receptions of the J-U-L were held in the month of July, so we all thought that that was a nice coincidence because the JUL receptions were held in July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Tanic. The point that needs to be clarified was whether the evidence you've just been giving about a discussion with Milosevic took place at a reception organised by the J-U-L party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The coalition party, in power together with us and Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us the approximate date of that reception?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, it was July 1997. But, as I have already said, Milosevic procrastinated a bit and said, "Well, let's negotiate a bit," and then, "Let's not." So it took him some time to come to the dismiss the negotiations in a political solution. He didn't take this decision overnight. He had problems with his associates, too. So he didn't dismiss this solution out of hand; it took him a while in the course of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you said at that reception that he said something to you about the number of Kosovo Albanians. What was that about?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, the problem appeared out of the blue, and Milosevic and associates of his, some who are now dead unfortunately, started saying that there were fewer than a million Albanians, under 10 percent of the total population of Serbia as a result. They claimed that they didn't have the right to consider themselves as a constituent people in Serbia and in Yugoslavia. They could only consider themselves as a minority. Seselj said that on one occasion, some of Milosevic's associates also said that. All of a sudden that issue became an important one, although it had not been previously discussed. But that wasn't true. There were far more than a million Albanians. When I said that there were more of them, there weren't two million of them, but there were at least a million and a half, or between 1.300.000 to a million and a half. And then he said, I'll demonstrate that there are under one million Albanians. But that was Milosevic; none of the gentlemen present here in the court ever mentioned that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask if you can explain for us a little bit about the significance of that. What difference does it make whether there were one million or one million and a half or 800.000? Why was that important?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, let me first say that I couldn't understand that either initially; and then I was provided with some explanations, according to which if they represent less than 10 percent, they can't be considered as a constituent people who would have the right to substantial autonomy. They can only be considered as a minority, so the Albanians were just an ethnic minority. And suddenly they started discussing the problem of Kosovo and not Kosovo Albanians. I didn't really look that case in, detail because it was clear to me that people from Milosevic's regime and Milosevic, himself, were trying to find a justification, a pretext, for that conflict, because it's not important whether there were 800.000 or 1.200.000 Kosovo Albanians. I didn't really see a difference; and then they started discussing other things that Broz's regime had given them 200.000 passports, that they had come from Albania. These arguments were characteristic for Milosevic's regime when the desire was to provoke a conflict. There were no rational arguments there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for those of us who might not know, you say Broz's regime, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, to the late president of Yugoslavia and the party leader, Josip Broz Tito. He was dead then; and then they started saying that Broz's regime had issued a lot of pass ports to Albanians so they could move into Kosovo, and they could artificially inflate the number of Albanians there. It is as if Broz was some sort of a traitor. It's something invented in cloud, cuckoo land.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Go to paragraph 27 of your statement. You indicate that although these negotiations were discreet and confidential, that, occasionally, there were newspaper articles about events related to the negotiations; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Gradually, we were preparing the public to understand that there were negotiations underway, that a political solution was possible. We sort of leaked articles to the public, and this included three interviews of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for the record, I won't put those up now to save time, but those listed in paragraph 27 is TX-2, TX-3, and TX-4 are exhibits P705, 706, and 707, respectively, for your review at a later time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 28, you describe the achievements of these discreet negotiations, and you make reference to the joint recommendations on the Kosovo conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could put up Exhibit P709.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tanic, if you could tell us briefly, what were the joint recommendations that came out as a result of these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, in fact they were identical to the initial political solution that Mihajlovic and myself had presented Milosevic, and Milosevic had approved it. So they were almost identical. That means that the international community had in fact accepted our position. So the idea was that there should be measures to re-establish trust, to have elections organised, to have joint security units, a tripartite or bilateral basis, the Serbians and Albanians or the Serbians, Albanians, and Keps [phoen]. This was in order to provide security, improve the security situation in the area. Elections were to be held. Transitory solution was to be found. They were supposed to be granted somewhat more autonomy than in 1974, than the autonomy they had in 1974, but their autonomy should be returned. And then later their status would be definitively solved. But naturally these recommendations were also of a practical kind. There was a series of practical recommendations. I wouldn't like to go into all of them, but some of them are recommendations I can no longer remember. So I'd have to examine the relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph number for this, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this 31?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think it's paragraph 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. It's document TX-6, which is Exhibit P709.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tanic, you say in your statement that these joint recommendations were the results of two meetings held on the island of Halki?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Not only those two meetings. This represents the result of the series of meetings and of consultations, at least 30 meetings were held. The Bertelsmann Foundation participated with Mr. Paglia and the European Union. Paglia also met Milosevic and Milutinovic, I believe. But that was later on, not at that time, since Mr. Milutinovic wasn't yet the minister of foreign affairs. Perhaps they did meet in Greece, however, I don't know. But nevertheless there were about 30 meetings; and yes, in technical terms, you might say that that's -- this represents the results of two meetings in Halki, one in Munich, one in Rhodes, and one in New York, to be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Milosevic implemented any of the proposals in this document?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, earlier on he had signed a proposal on education, which was part of those measures for re-establishing trust; that was the first stage. And then other measures were to be taken to re-establish trust, to reinforce trust, but this wasn't done. He didn't sign this with me or in my presence. He signed this with Rugova through the intermediary of Monsignor Paglia. He was from a paradiplomatic association, the community of San Edigio. He had a contact group involved in his work, and he often met with me and Milosevic, and then they signed that agreement on education. There was just this one measure that was taken in order to reinforce trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for the record that is Exhibit 715, which has been presented in the court previously to other witnesses, including Mr. Surroi. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I want to move forward in your statement to paragraph 43 and 44. Now we're moving in time to October of 1998. You talk about the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement in October of 1998, which you describe as implementing some of the things that had been recommended previously in the joint recommendations. In paragraph 44, you say: "After concluding this agreement with Holbrooke, Milosevic sent Serb negotiators to Kosovo 13 times to discuss the autonomy of the province and not of the Kosovo Albanians." Can you explain for the Judges what the significance, if any, there is to this difference between autonomy of the province versus autonomy of the Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, if you have an autonomous province, well, that didn't mean much for the Kosovo Albanians, because they wanted to enjoy their right to self-determination in a certain sense after the break-up of the former Yugoslavia. And regardless of how far they wanted to go down the route of self-determination, regardless of whether they wanted a semi-solution or whether they were going to stand by their most rigid positions, well, the autonomy of Kosovo really didn't provide them with a way of meeting their right to self-determination. And it, in fact, created the conditions for manipulation. But, yes, the agreement with Holbrooke is almost identical to the spirit of these agreements -- well, Holbrooke was naturally familiar with the way the negotiations were going. We had, naturally, contact with the American ambassador. When I say "we," I mean Mihajlovic, myself. We also had contact with state department representatives. So easy for them and Milosevic to sign that because they knew that such an agreement existed, but it wasn't his intention to implement it. Then all of a sudden there was the problem of the autonomy of Kosovo Albanians that was transferred into him into the autonomy of the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there to ask you a question. You say it was easy for Milosevic to sign that, but it wasn't his intention to implement it. What do you base that on? How do you know that, that it was not his intention?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, according to all the information that we had through political intelligence and personal contacts, well- and this is the reason for which we left the coalition government, the New Democracy left the coalition with Milosevic, because we saw that he and his associates was deceiving people at home and abroad. He would pretend that he wanted a political solution. He was deceiving his associates by saying that there was no political solution, whereas there was. He wanted us to procrastinate to see what we would do, and this all reminded us of his rhetoric that he had used earlier. And we, as a party, myself, Mihajlovic, and others from the core party, when we saw that he and his regime wanted to provoke one more war, well, at that point in time we said, "This really isn't necessary. There's a political agreement. If you want a war, then you can wage it yourself or with the JUL."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not really an answer to this question, Mr. Tanic. Mr. Hannis wants to know how you came to the conclusion that he was not going to implement or had no intention of implementing it. It's easy to say, but what is your basis for coming to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't draw any conclusions. I was working on the basis of information. The information was such that there was no agreement. He had signed an agreement with Holbrooke just to buy time. That was information we received through the State Security Service and through the political establishment. Secondly, given Milosevic's behaviour, well, he agreed on the autonomy of Kosovo Albanians with Holbrooke. But two days after that agreement, he started sending negotiators to discuss the autonomy of Kosovo. And this immediately demonstrated the fact that he wouldn't accept the agreement. Thirdly, we had clear information according to which he was preparing for war. He was storing equipment. He had started creating decoys, model tanks, model artillery, et cetera. Why would you engage in such activities if you were prepared to implement an agreement? And, finally, on a number of occasions, Milosevic told me and Mihajlovic, "If you don't feel good about this" -- he said this when Mihajlovic or I would criticise him. He said, or rather, he told Mihajlovic - I think I was present, too - he told Mihajlovic, "If you don't feel good here, you can leave." That means if you don't want to accept a war, leave. All of this information is reliable. We're talking about a process, not an event that took place on Thursday, the 24th of July, of such and such a year. This is a process that lasted over a number of months. Milosevic and his associates needed some time to take the decision to go to war. For that reason, Milosevic also had problems with Stanisic and Perisic, because they were also against this option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't be so dismissive of the questions that are asked of you. You have, in fact, answered that question in precisely the way I anticipated by indicating material from which you have drawn conclusions, as well as referring to the information you received. So we now have a clear understanding of the position and an actual answer to the question that was asked. We are now into what I have to confess I find difficulty territory of political theory about constituent peoples and the right to self-determination. And I know that in the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- sorry, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, there was a concept of constituent peoples. But was there such a concept in the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, no, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So -- can I stop you there. Where then does this idea come from that if you've got 10 percent of the population, you are a constituent people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I have already said, this was one of the irrational [Realtime transcript read in error "rational"] justifications that I had heard. Milosevic and his associates would just come up with these justifications. I was quite surprised by what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, again the transcript. I believe the witness said the irrational, 68, 7, irrational justifications that I had heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, did you describe the justification as irrational or as rational?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Irrational, irrational.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said your party -- you said "we," your party, New Democracy then left. Is this the point in time you left the coalition with the SPS and JUL?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we became persuaded on the basis of all the information we were receiving, not just on the basis of the information I had, but on the basis of the information that our party leader had and other party members, when we became persuaded that Milosevic and his associates wanted to provoke a new war in Kosovo and when we became persuaded that he thought there was no political solution, whereas there was a political solution, we then left the coalition. And I apologise if you seem to think that some of my answers were perhaps dismissive that these are very emotive issues for me because my country suffered a lot for no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you. In several of your recent answers you referred to Milosevic and his associates, but can you be more specific who you are referring to as his associates in the context of these most recent answers that you've given.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, when I myself am concerned -- well, that was Jovica Stanisic, through Zoran Mijatovic I received a message from Mr. Stanisic, as the head of the State Security Service at the time. And according to this message -- he said, "Well, the boss doesn't want to hear about that. We're done with the political solution." He said Jovica Stanisic had problems with Milosevic because he wanted to provoke a war in Kosovo. Stanisic was against this. So I was told to be careful, to watch myself and distance myself from that issue to the extent it was possible. So Jovica Stanisic was one of Milosevic's associates, and he confirmed this to me through Zoran Mijatovic. As far as Mihajlovic and myself are concerned, well, I don't know what channels Mihajlovic had. I assume he had direct channels to Milosevic. On one or two occasions, Mr. Milutinovic said this to us, too, in a far more civilised way. Since Mr. Milutinovic is a different kind of person in comparison -- when compared to Milosevic, I don't think he was happy about the war. But we also heard from him that the political solution wasn't functioning. Mr. Milutinovic tried to show us that the western forces wanted to deceive us, that they wouldn't allow us entry into the EU, even if we achieved a political solution with the Kosovo Albanians. So these would be the associates I was referring to. Mr. Jovica Stanisic, Zoran Mijatovic, Milutinovic, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The difficulty for me with that, Mr. Tanic, is that each one of these persons you've indicated had a different view from Milosevic, and what Mr. Hannis is after is identifying who the associates of Milosevic were that wanted a war along with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Milosevic gave us that information. We didn't obtain that much information from his associates; we obtained far more information from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's you that used the expression, "Milosevic and his associates wanted another war." Now, who are these associates? You'll understand my reason for asking the question, bearing in mind who the accused are in this case and what this case is all about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as the accused are concerned in this case, the associates were Milutinovic and Sainovic, naturally. Mr. Milutinovic didn't approve of Mr. Milosevic's reasons, but he supported his idea that they should go to war and Mr. Sainovic was actively involved in provoking that war. I don't have direct information from Mr. Sainovic about that, but I have very reliable information from the State Security Service that had quite a lot of problems with Mr. Sainovic. And they told me that he was pretty involved in provoking a war in Kosovo. That's as far as the accused are concerned here. There are other people, some are dead now, such as Vlajko Stojiljkovic. I also had several conversations with him and there are colleagues of mine. Admiral Jokic, who had been sentenced here. He admitted that he had shelled Dubrovnik. He was a member of the New Democracy council. Then there were the heads of military and intelligence services. They were all members of our council --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, please restrain yourself also. The events in Dubrovnik were long before what we are talking about here, and to draw that sort of conclusion, without a foundation, is not assisting the process of this trial. Mr. Hannis will endeavour to elaborate if he feels it necessary. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, yeah, let me ask you a question about that. You mentioned Admiral Jokic in this connection. Did he have anything to do with the -- what you described as Milosevic and his associates wanting to have a war with regard to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he didn't have anything to do with it, but he had reliable information. Members of your presidential council were, among others, Aleksandar Vasiljevic, former; and then he was to become head of the state security; Milanovic, the former chief of the Serbian army. I wanted to say that we had a number of information channels, both Mr. Mihajlovic and I. This wasn't just one person. There were many of them; that's why I used the term "Milosevic's associates." Other than that, Mr. Jokic has nothing to do with Kosovo. I apologise in that respect. I just referred to him by way of illustration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me see if I can clear this up a bit then. You're describing Admiral Jokic as one of the persons who was a source of information for you about Milosevic and some of his other associates wanting a war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, because Mr. Jokic, as did the other Milosevic's associates, describe Milosevic's strategy of provoking a war earlier on. In my statement I said how I came by information. I obtained information on three levels. It wasn't just accidental eavesdropping in a hotel or wherever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go back to where I was a few moments ago. When New Democracy left the coalition, do you recall approximately what date that occurred?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: We abandoned the coalition within a process, again. We held several closed sessions and then one public session. Mr. Mihajlovic and I wrote a national platform where we described Milosevic's regime along the lines that we were mentioning now. This was in 1997, and then we passed decisions along the party bodies that we would no longer form part of the coalition. We left the coalition, and then there were some elections which we did not participate in because there was the joint parties of SPS, New Democracy, and JUL before. So we simply parted ways in a civilised way, through the meetings that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the course of doing that, did you or Mr. Mihajlovic or New Democracy, as a party, bring to Mr. Milosevic's attention why you were leaving in respect of it being because you saw him as preparing for a war? ?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, on several occasions, to him and Milutinovic. I don't know whether Mihajlovic spoke to Sainovic directly or through some mediators. I can't say. I believe he did, but I can't confirm that. I know that we spoke to Milosevic on several occasions. We sent messages and fax -- facsimiles. We also spoke to Milutinovic. Through the State Security Service, I also sent information anticipating this, and I also anticipated the attack by NATO on Serbia because of the exacerbation of the situation with the Kosovo Albanians. Milosevic and Milutinovic rejected that, but of course Milutinovic did this in quite a different way, in a very polite way, as saying that we were wrong in thinking that, whereas Milosevic was quite brutal. Now, as for Sainovic, I believe Mihajlovic told me that he tried to speak to him two or three times. I really can't say at this time whether he did talk to him. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did New Democracy make any kind of public pronouncement at a press conference or in the media about why they were leaving the coalition?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did. There were a number of press conferences where, to the extent we were allowed, we explained our reasons. Had we listed all the reasons, we were would have lost our lives at the time. But I said that Mihajlovic and I wrote a booklet, where we clearly laid out what Milosevic's regime was doing. We held several press conferences, and I gave several interviews. It was a public parting. Everyone knew that New Democracy did not support Milosevic's preparations for the provoking of a new war, this time in Kosovo. And we -- our prediction that this would lead to the NATO attack was true. I directed his attention to this through the State Security Service, and the answer I received back was that I was simply being fed misinformation by someone so that he might, in turn, be misled. Milutinovic didn't believe that there would come a -- such an attack either, but I have to make a distinction between them. He was never -- he supported Milosevic's ideas, but I don't believe that he was the mastermind behind it all at any point or that he himself wished for these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me move on to another topic. In 1997/1998, did you become aware of any international offers to Serbia to help deal with the problem of the Albanian terrorist or the UCK? First of all, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, but before 1997; therefore, in this period but before 1997 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you learn about these offers, from whom?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Credible diplomatic sources of Great Britain, Italy, United States, Germany, then from among intelligence services, the British intelligence service. And when we matched the information our service had, they tallied, plus there was the Russian diplomacy as well. They all contacted us as the junior partner in the government in an attempt to help solve the problem of terrorism in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say "our service as well," do you mean the SDB?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, the SDB had information consistent with my information to the effect that western countries were prepared to help Milosevic to solve the problem of terrorism in exchange for a political settlement with Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the information you learned about the nature of the offer to Mr. Milosevic to reach a political settlement with the Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: It was -- well, along the lines of the three phases that I mentioned. The confidence-building measures. It was called the substantial autonomy or substantive. They also offered technical solutions for border control. That would have been the electronical border control and other solutions that would reduce the risk of Albanian terrorists. And you have to keep in mind that in 1995/1996, they were still abroad. The offers were quite credible and they were conveyed to Milosevic through other channels as well, as well as to him personally. Therefore, not just through me. I don't want you to get the wrong impression that I'm trying to exaggerate the role I had. The offers were not passed only through me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you aware of what Mr. Milosevic's response was to these offers?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: I can talk about my experience. For the most part, he ignored them. Once or twice, he even rejected them. As for other offers, I can only tell you what I indirectly know, what I learned from diplomats who confirmed this to me. In conversations he seemed agreeable, but when it came to the implementation stage he rejected the implementations. He didn't even wanted the security service to locate the KLA terrorists abroad. He even obstructed that line of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objection. I just don't know whether Mr. Hannis is still following the statement or are we following something else because I can't find this in the statement. Is this still paragraph 45 of the statement or have we gone past that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've gone past that, Your Honour. I'm now into portions of the statement that are not in evidence. If Mr. Fila wants to follow, I can tell him that I'm in paragraph 47 of the full statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we have gone back in time, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. May I receive this extended statement? I only have 45 paragraphs of my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has decided to allow the Prosecution to present your evidence in writing up to paragraph 45 of the statement, but thereafter we wish to hear what you have to say from your own personal knowledge. So that statement is not part of the evidence in the case beyond paragraph 45. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in your last answer that you learned some of this information from diplomats, who confirmed it to you. Can you tell us who any of those individuals were?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, ambassadors of the countries I mentioned. I had regular contacts with them. Of course there were individuals abroad; and for reasons that are quite understandable, these are members of the British intelligence service, I cannot name them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I have just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did the -- did the SDB, to your knowledge, have a position about these offers from the west to assist in dealing with the problem of Albanian terrorism or Kosovo Albanian terrorism?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: But of course. They supported it with all their might; however, Milosevic obstructed them and he had Sainovic assisting him in that and other associates. I can mention them. And he tied up their hands in other ways as well. I can tell you about it. This was one of the reasons why Jovica Stanisic started suspecting that Milosevic didn't want to solve the Kosovo problem at all, but rather that he wanted to create a new war. Milosevic's regime seemed to have protected Albanian terrorists from -- and shielding them from any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You just said that Mr. Sainovic was assisting in -- him in that. Can you tell us in what ways he was assisting the obstruction of accepting or using these offers from the international community.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: According to the information I received from the service- and I have no reason to doubt the credibility of the information- Mr. Sainovic interfered with the service of the police in two or three different ways. One way was that he conveyed personal Milosevic's messages that were contradictory to the actual situation on the ground and quite often they went against our law. Secondly, whenever he was able to learn about some actions about the SDB, he tried to, in order to be able to misrepresent their reports or to have an impact on these reports. This is information I had -- I received from the SDB. I didn't have any personal dealings with Sainovic ever, but I do not doubt the authenticity of the information; they are highly credible. This is the helicopter incidents, the establishing of the actual situation in Kosovo, various recordings that were made. Sainovic was one of the people obstructing the work of our security service and police, upon Milosevic's orders, in order to create on impression that the Kosovo situation could not be solved by any means other than the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and ask you if you can clarify part of your answer. You mention the helicopter incidents. What are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Perisic and Sainovic [as interpreted] wanted to organise a fact-finding mission in Kosovo. Both of them were opposed to Milosevic's provoking the war, and they hoped that they themselves, and through Lenic they would be, or rather, through Lenic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would be able to have an impact on Milosevic's thinking. All at once as they were about to set off on that mission Sainovic got on the helicopter. And according to the information I received from both Perisic and Stanisic, he -- the situation was quite different in his presence. All of a sudden, the reports on the situation on the ground were different. Sainovic later on, with Milosevic, accused the security service for the chaos in Kosovo. There were even stories about the security service and police being involved in drug trafficking with the Albanians in Kosovo. They simply wanted to establish the situation on the ground and to propose measures by which the Albanian terrorism would be halted, because by that time it had gained a much greater hand. It had gone a bit out of hand. So this is just one example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two matters there arising in the transcript. Page 78, line 18, I think is a reference to Perisic and Stanisic, not Sainovic. And one other matter I'd like you to clarify, Mr. Tanic, you said Sainovic was one of the people obstructing the work of your security service and people on Milosevic's orders, in order to create an impression that something could not be involved by any means other than the war. What did you say there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, it is true, I meant --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true. I meant Perisic and Stanisic. Now, as for Sainovic, the information I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop there. Let's simplify it and if it's not going to be easy for you to answer. Did you actually refer to the terrorist situation in Kosovo could not be resolved other than by war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I'm not sure that answered to your question, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, did you mean that the terrorist situation in Kosovo could not be resolved by any other means than by war?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: This isn't what I thought or Perisic or Stanisic, but Sainovic was working toward creating the impression as if there is no other solution than war. And in that sense, he distorted information flowing to Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand -- Mr. Tanic, I understand that but in the transcript it said the Kosovo problem or situation, I can't now remember. But did you not actually say the position of terrorism in Kosovo. You actually mentioned terrorism in your answer, or is that not the case? I just want to be clear if you used the word "terrorism."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies the situation. And you're attributing that wish or idea to Sainovic, we understand that. But it was the use of the word that was important for the transcript. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, we were just talking about offers from the west to assist Serbia with the problem of Albanian terrorism in Kosovo, and you said SDB was in favour of that. But when it was turned down or declined by Mr. Milosevic, did the SDB itself have some alternative plan at that time for how to deal with the problem of Albanian terrorism?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Yes, the SDB and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was that plan, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: At the time, and we are talking about 1998 now, when the situation in Kosovo was worse than at the time of the negotiations, both services, the SDB and the army and definitely also the police, were in favour of the declaration of a state of emergency in Kosovo, because that would make it possible to legally employ the police and army in fighting terrorism and to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the second matter that he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second, the final negotiations with the international community were opened where Milutinovic started acting as the person who also conveyed distorted information. This is what Sainovic did at home and Milutinovic did abroad. They asked -- they wanted the definitive negotiating process to be opened up with the Americans and the European Union. And, thirdly, they -- well, a political settlement had already been passed for that, because they said that if in the absence of a political settlement, the terrorists would multiply because they would have a pretext for that and nobody would be able to win them. The service and the army also had some specific technical solutions for that, but I wouldn't talk about them in open session. These are not pleasant solutions, but, of course, when faced with terrorists they cannot be. Milosevic did not want to accept any of these. In addition, the SDB and the army wanted to expand the area which they would control by ten kilometres. Milosevic didn't want this. They asked for electronic equipment for surveying the borders, for monitoring the borders. But Milosevic was opposed to that as well, and there was no equipment arriving at any point. Simply put, together with his associates, Milosevic raised the issue of the Albanian terrorism to a level which did not correspond to reality; and both Sainovic and Milutinovic had a hand in that, the former one at home and the latter one abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you about something you mentioned earlier when you explained to me about the helicopter incident. You described a fact-finding mission. In February or March of 1998, was there some sort of governmental effort to find out or get a better idea about the nature of the problem of terrorism in Kosovo. Who organised that, and what was the objective? How were they going to achieve it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraphs 52 and 53.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Microphone, please, again. Well, the state took certain steps -- or I should say Milosevic's regime made some efforts, but they were more declarative than substantial. He set up a state commission for the Kosovo issue; this was Minic, Sainovic, Lukic, and others. Practically, by doing so, he took up the entire Kosovo issue from the hands of the legal organs; the police, state security, and army. These efforts to solve the problems of terrorism in Kosovo -- well, I cannot even describe them as efforts because certain police actions, which were conducted under the instructions from Belgrade, were conducted in such a way that our police suffered losses and Albanian civilians got killed or wounded. And this cannot be termed as an effort. It is true that by forming the commission, he --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. I did not phrase my question very clearly, I guess. You had mentioned the helicopter incident and the fact-finding mission that Mr. -- I think you said Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Perisic were going on. That is what I meant to ask you about. Were you aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Stanisic and Perisic, as the chief of the security service and the chief of the military, well, they wanted to examine the situation in the field and to see what the situation was; and then to make suggestions to Milosevic, so that they could have a basis upon which the state could try to solve the problem. But they weren't able to do anything with Mr. Sainovic in their company. I knew something about that mission, but not much. I knew about Perisic's and Stanisic's efforts. And as far as this [indiscernible] is concerned, I knew something about it. I knew about the conflict between Stanisic and Milosevic through the service. I knew about the details. But as far as the helicopter incident is concerned, I only heard something about it at the time, and this was later confirmed by Perisic. As far as the military problems and Milosevic, I found out about that later. But as far as the service are concerned, I had detailed information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said Stanisic and Perisic weren't able to do anything with Mr. Sainovic in their company. What led you to that conclusion? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, that was their opinion, naturally my opinion, too. If they are coming to a joint conclusion as to the situation in the field, well Sainovic is there, too, and naturally the conclusions will be the conclusions that Milosevic wants. They won't reflect the actual situation in the field. The conclusions under the influence of Sainovic were catastrophic. It turned out that our soldiers in the security service were in fact the cause of terrorism in Kosovo. I'm saying this in a somewhat cavalier manner, but that's how things looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this. If we look at the last ten or 15 lines of the transcript, the witness is saying he's got second- or third-hand information, coupled with details he doesn't know about; someone's opinion, which is a bit like his opinion as well. It's inadmissible hearsay. It's conjecture and speculation and shouldn't be allowed to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, see, Mr. Hannis, the witness himself has described this as rather cavalier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can ask a couple other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your answer to my question about what led you to conclude that Stanisic and Perisic weren't able to do anything with Mr. Sainovic in their company on that fact-finding mission, was -- that was their opinion. How do you know that was their opinion?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR TANIC
utterances.text: Well, you know the chief of the State Security Service and the head of the military, well, this isn't second- or third-hand information. We constantly exchanged our opinions, and Jovica Stanisic via Zoran Mijatovic told me the number of occasions that they had many problems with Sainovic, and that Sainovic wanted to misrepresent the information that was going from Milosevic to the police and to the Serbs and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, let's concentrate on the question you've been asked. You see, you're dealing with a particular situation, that the trip wasn't going to be worthwhile. Now, can you concentrate on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course, of course. I was told that by Jovica Stanisic through Zoran Mijatovic. I knew about the trip and so did Mihajlovic. But we didn't really look into the matter at the time, because we weren't in power. I wasn't describing something that I didn't know about. Later General Perisic confirmed the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is -- although you say it's not second- or third-hand hearsay, in fact it's both second- and third-hand hearsay. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan, you now know the basis for this, which is said to come from two sources, one third-hand and one second-hand hearsay. Do you still maintain your objection now that we know the precise details, and bearing in mind that you can cross-examine this?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In my respectful submission, this isn't the kind of evidence that should be led. The point's been clarified, and we will have a chance to cross-examine. But as a more -- as a preliminary point, in my submission, which is whether or not this sort of evidence should be heard by the Trial Chamber at all. There's no foundation for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you telling me there is some authority that would exclude this?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. I can refer you to the Aleksovski Appeals Chamber decision on -- which we cited in our motion in relation to this witness already. Now, we know as a general proposition that hearsay is admissible. And if you give me a moment, I'll give you a more specific reference. Well, maybe I won't. The Aleksovski Appeals Chamber decision says that the Trial Chamber has discretion whether or not to admit hearsay evidence. There must be indicia of reliable. There must be foundation for that, whether it's first-, second-, third-hand hearsay. In addition, the Appeals Chamber has stated -- now I have the reference to the decision. It's Prosecutor versus Aleksovski; decision on the Prosecutor's appeal on admissibility of evidence, 16 February 1999, paragraph 14, IT-95-14/1A. And there the Appeals Chamber is saying that you must consider both the content and the trustworthiness of the circumstances under which the evidence arose. And we say that with this witness and this particular form of hearsay, which he's offering, that there's a -- has not been proof, or it has not been established by the Prosecution that there's any basis for this to be trustworthy information. The context in Tadic, which is the basis of hearsay, is one that is quite different. There, it's people with shared experiences, people who lived through the same events, some of whom did not survive, may have told an individual who recounts it. Someone who actually lived and shared the experience; this is not the case with this witness. And we say that Aleksovski provides a basis for you to exercise your discretion and not allow this type of evidence to be heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, one of his answers was that General Perisic later confirmed this to him. I would argue that that's first-hand hearsay, and that is -- that's about as close as we can get, short of having General Perisic here. We know that General Perisic is a person. We know that General Perisic was in the army. We have evidence that he did go on that mission. We'll have an exhibit from him where he complained what was being done with the army and about how things were being done in Kosovo that are in conformity of being disappointed on the fact-finding mission. And he was -- he and Mr. Stanisic both were replaced from their positions, not a long time after this, we say because of disagreements with what Mr. Milosevic was doing. So it's consistent with that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say you'll have an exhibit from Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We have a letter that he wrote to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- Mr. Milosevic that has been published in a book and was led as evidence in Milosevic and is, I think, not strongly disputed that it is his letter to Mr. Milosevic about the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll consider the authorities that have been referred to, since I -- the point pervades this evidence. It's not just related to this one passage. And we'll give a decision first thing on Monday. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecutor had just said that they have an exhibit on that helicopter flight. Perisic, Stanisic, and Sainovic were allegedly in that helicopter. This never took place, so I would like to see the exhibit referred to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, that's not what he said. He's talking about a --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there is a letter written by Perisic that has nothing to do with the helicopter. The helicopter isn't mentioned in that letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, I don't think Mr. Hannis suggested it was. I am --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. It has to do with recommendations he made after the fact-finding mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. In any event, we don't have time at the moment to deal with anything arising from that. Mr. Tanic, we now have to interrupt. That brings our proceedings for the week to an end, and you will require to return on Monday to continue with your evidence. I need to check at what time on Monday, 9.00. So it will be first thing on Monday morning, 9.00, ready to resume here at that time. We'll now go into closed session to enable you to leave the court. Over the weekend it is vital, Mr. Tanic, that you have no discussion with anyone about any aspect of your evidence, either the evidence you've given or the evidence you've yet to give. You can talk about anything else that you wish to with anybody you wish to, but you must keep off, absolutely off, the subject of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of November, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
